name: Folic acid
short: Cancer: 6 pooled trials found higher incidence (RR 1.21); 13 pooled trials found no significant effect. On phenytoin, if folate-deficient: lower phenytoin levels, possible loss of seizure control.
text: Two reviews of the phenytoin and folic acid interaction (1984 and 1995) report that giving folic acid to folate-deficient patients with epilepsy who take phenytoin lowered serum phenytoin concentrations, with possible loss of seizure control or seizure breakthrough, while long-term phenytoin itself depletes folate; the 1995 review reported that starting the two together prevents the fall in folate and lets phenytoin reach steady state sooner. In contrast, a Cochrane review of small trials of poor methodological quality in epilepsy (nine studies with 331 participants tested folic acid) found no consistent changes in serum phenytoin or phenobarbitone levels with folic acid; two studies (75 participants) found no effect for the outcome of a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, and the abstract does not report whether seizures became more frequent. On high intakes, a 2024 review states that high-dose folic acid (over 5 mg a day), used in the 1940s and 1950s for pernicious anaemia, masked vitamin B12 deficiency and possibly worsened its neurological progression, and that high-dose folic acid in patients with pernicious anaemia or epilepsy caused significant falls in serum B12; it describes this evidence as primarily correlative or from uncontrolled observations. For cancer, a meta-analysis of six large supplementation trials reported higher cancer incidence with folic acid (relative risk 1.21), whereas a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (49,406 participants) found no significant effect on total cancer incidence (relative risk 1.05) or on cancer mortality, and a lower risk of melanoma; in a subgroup finding across trials, total cancer incidence was higher in trials where more than 60% of participants used lipid-lowering drugs (relative risk 1.10). No other interaction data were found in the cited sources.
